description:
We are an independent team of high school students from Türkiye with a strong interest in software development, artificial intelligence, data science, and space exploration.

Our goal is to combine our technical skills, creativity, and teamwork to develop innovative solutions to real-world challenges using NASA's open data and resources.

We are passionate about learning, experimenting with new technologies, and turning ambitious ideas into practical solutions.
summary: When a crew is on its way to Mars, Earth can be up to 22 minutes away by radio. SpaceApp Logar is an offline-first, explainable health decision-support system for astronauts. It continuously checks 12 vital and cabin telemetry streams, real NASA OSDR Inspiration4 lab data and crew check-ins against 11 deterministic rules across NASA's five spaceflight hazards. Every alert says why, distinguishes sensor faults from physiological change ("unknown is not normal") and opens a reasoned action card. Alerts are shown on a clickable 3D anatomy body map. ALERT and CRITICAL events are escalated automatically to the flight surgeon as signed, hash-checked packets, and an Earth mission-control console shows when the ground could see each event under real light delay (ISS, Moon or Mars mission profile). The system never diagnoses and never suggests medication. Only the CO2 rule uses a published NASA threshold (NASA-STD-3001); every other threshold is labelled DEMO.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

On the way to Mars, Earth can be up to 22 minutes away by radio, and a solar conjunction can cut the link entirely. SpaceApp Logar is an offline-first, explainable health decision-support system that helps a non-physician crew decide what to do now, and tells Earth what happened in a verifiable way.

- Data in: 12 vital and cabin telemetry streams (heart rate, SpO2, respiration, temperature, blood pressure, sleep, HRV; cabin CO2, O2, pressure, radiation), crew check-ins, red-flag symptom reports, real NASA OSDR Inspiration4 lab values and manual lab entry.

- Explainable rule engine: 11 deterministic, versioned rules across NASA's five spaceflight hazards plus a data-reliability check. Multi-signal rules combine evidence (resting heart rate + respiration + symptoms; cabin CO2 + reported headache). Every alert shows the measured value, threshold, time window, data quality, evidence class and source.

- Unknown is not normal: sensor dropouts and implausible jumps are labelled FAULT or SUSPECT; missing data makes the status UNKNOWN, never "normal". Personal baselines and declared activity (rest, exercise, sleep) keep context honest.

- Action cards, not prescriptions: step-by-step cards give a reason for every step, a reassessment timer, escalation and closing conditions, and a live situation block. Red-flag symptoms (e.g. chest pain) open a CRITICAL alert immediately.

- 3D anatomy body map: a realistic BodyParts3D body with nine regions coloured by attention level (colour + icon + text). Click a region to see its rules, latest values and open alerts.

- Ground link: delay-tolerant packets are routed automatically to the flight surgeon, life support, radiation team and mission control, protected by SHA-256 hashes and HMAC-SHA256 signatures. Every ALERT/CRITICAL alert automatically creates a priority escalation for the flight surgeon; the ground acknowledges by hash.

- Mission profiles (ISS / Moon / Mars): the light delay changes who owns the decision. If Earth's round trip is longer than the action window, the action card hands the decision to the onboard crew medical officer. An Earth mission-control console shows ship and Earth timelines side by side under real light delay (display-only simulation, clearly labelled).

BENEFITS

- The crew gets a clear, reasoned next step in seconds, without waiting for Earth.

- Trust: every alert can be traced to a rule, a threshold, the data behind it and its evidence class. Nothing is a black box.

- Fewer false alarms: in our labelled synthetic validation (7 scenario families, N=15 each) the engine flagged every injected event, raised 0/15 false alerts on normal windows versus 10/15 for a naive fixed-threshold baseline, and reported UNKNOWN instead of a false alert on every sensor-fault window. This is synthetic data, not clinical validation.

- Earth stays informed: integrity-checked, routed packets and automatic escalation mean the right ground team sees the right event, and everyone can see when they could have seen it.

INTENDED IMPACT

Long-duration missions to the Moon and Mars need crews that can act autonomously and safely. SpaceApp Logar shows how decision support can stay explainable, honest about uncertainty and accountable to the ground. The same pattern applies on Earth to remote and austere settings (polar stations, ships, rural clinics) where a specialist is far away or offline.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES AND SOFTWARE

- Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, Alembic (18 migrations), SQLite or PostgreSQL, signed demo tokens with three roles (astronaut, crew medical officer, ground).

- Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Three.js / React Three Fiber; fully offline at run time (no CDN, embedded fonts).

- Quality: 400+ automated tests, GitHub Actions CI (SQLite, PostgreSQL 16, frontend build) and a CI guard that fails the build if diagnosis or medication wording appears.

- Deployment: multi-stage Docker and a Render blueprint. No special hardware: data adapters accept CSV/JSON telemetry from wearables and cabin sensors.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

- It treats light delay as a design input: the mission profile decides whether Earth or the onboard medical officer owns a decision.

- "Unknown is not normal" is built into the engine and the UI, so faulty sensors never hide behind a green light.

- A clickable 3D anatomy map turns rule results into something a non-physician understands at a glance.

- A guided one-click tour plays a whole incident: CO2 + headache → body map → action card → automatic escalation → signed packet → delayed Earth console → acknowledgement.

- Every value carries a source badge: REAL (NASA OSDR, PhysioNet, NASA DONKI), STANDARD (NASA-STD-3001), DEMO or SYNTHETIC.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Safety and honesty: the system never diagnoses and never suggests medication. Only the cabin CO2 rule uses a published NASA threshold (NASA-STD-3001); every other threshold is labelled DEMO and needs flight-medicine validation. Demo vitals are synthetic and labelled.

- Data quality and missing data, communication blackouts, integrity and authentication of ground packets, accessibility (colour is never the only signal, keyboard support, reduced motion), and running fully offline.

- Known limits stated openly: BodyParts3D has no lung tissue or inner-ear labyrinth, so lungs are shown as airways and vessels and the inner-ear region uses the external ear; radiation event timing comes from NASA DONKI while dose values are synthetic.

AI USE

AI coding assistants (Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Google Antigravity) helped write code, tests and documentation; parallel AI coding agents implemented parts of the backend and the React dashboard. The team set the requirements and product limits, reviewed and merged the work. No AI runs inside the decision engine: all rules, thresholds and action cards are fixed, deterministic and versioned.

Live demo: https://spaceapp-logar.onrender.com/ui/ (one-click demo login; free hosting may need about a minute to wake up)

Source code: https://github.com/zynordev/spaceapp-logar
